thousands of GPUs for weeks. Not a platform team's job.
Going deeper2 points
  • Training becomes worth it when large, slow-changing knowledge would otherwise ride along in every prompt. Long contexts cost GPU memory on every request, so a bank might bake lending and risk knowledge into a model and keep RAG for fresh facts.
  • Smaller and specialized often beats bigger and general: a small model (8–16B parameters), possibly distilled from a large one, can match a big general model on one task at a fraction of the serving cost.

Full fine-tuning vs. LoRA

Scenario. The team has 800 labelled examples of support replies in the company's tone. A full fine-tune of a 7B model needs several large GPUs, far more examples than they have, and produces a second 15 GB model to serve. They need something smaller.

What the picture shows. What each method trains, and what it costs.

1Full fine-tuning
updates every weight. It needs hundreds of thousands of labelled examples and many GPUs (the optimizer state alone is several times the model size), risks "catastrophic forgetting" of general skills, and produces a separate full model that needs its own GPUs to serve.
2LoRA (low-rank adaptation)
freezes the base model and trains two small matrices per adapted layer, often under 1% of the parameters. It needs only 100–1,000 good examples and finishes in hours on one or a few GPUs.
3The adapter is small
tens to a few hundred MB, stored and versioned separately from the base model.
4QLoRA
loads the frozen base model in 4 bits during training, which cuts training memory further so larger models fit on smaller GPUs.
5Newer methods
(DPO for preferences, GRPO, reward modelling) show up as multi-step pipelines with several GPU components, not a single job.

The code. A LoRA fine-tune with Hugging Face PEFT and TRL's SFTTrainer.

from datasets import load_datasetfrom peft import LoraConfigfrom trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer dataset = load_dataset("json", data_files="/data/support-replies.jsonl", split="train")  # 800 chats peft_config = LoraConfig(    r=16,                                   # rank: size of the adapter matrices    lora_alpha=32,    lora_dropout=0.05,    target_modules=["q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"],   # attention projections    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",) trainer = SFTTrainer(    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct",       # base weights stay frozen    train_dataset=dataset,    peft_config=peft_config,    args=SFTConfig(        output_dir="/checkpoints/support-tone",   # on a PVC: survives restarts        num_train_epochs=3,        per_device_train_batch_size=4,        gradient_accumulation_steps=4,        learning_rate=2e-4,        bf16=True,        save_steps=100,    ),)trainer.train()trainer.save_model("/checkpoints/support-tone/final")   # a ~100 MB adapter, not a 15 GB model
Going deeper2 points
  • Data quality beats quantity for LoRA. 500 clean, representative examples usually beat 5,000 noisy ones. Hold out a test set, and evaluate the adapter with the same pipeline as any model (see Running LLMs in production).
  • Merge or keep separate? An adapter can be merged into the base weights for a single-purpose deployment. Keeping it separate lets one base model serve many adapters, which is the next section.

Serving many adapters on one base model

Scenario. Ten teams each fine-tuned an adapter on the same 7B base model. Serving each as its own full model would take ten GPUs that sit mostly idle. They want all ten on two replicas.

What the picture shows. One base model in GPU memory, many adapters loaded beside it, and routing that knows which replica has which adapter.

1One copy of the base weights
per replica, shared by every adapter.
2Adapters loaded side by side
vLLM keeps several adapters in GPU memory and applies the right one per request; the request's model field names the adapter.
3Batching across adapters
requests for different adapters run in the same batch, so the GPU stays busy even when each team's traffic is small.
4LoRA-aware routing
when there are more adapters than fit on one replica, the gateway sends each request to a replica that already has its adapter loaded. See kube-proxy: iptables vs. IPVS for how inference-aware routing works.

The YAML. A vLLM server with LoRA enabled and two adapters registered at startup (container arguments).

args:- --model=Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct- --enable-lora- --max-loras=8                                         # adapters in GPU memory at once- --max-lora-rank=16- --lora-modules- support-tone=/adapters/support-tone                   # name=path; request with model="support-tone"- legal-summary=/adapters/legal-summary
Going deeper2 points
  • Adapters are just files. Package them as small OCI image layers on top of the base model, so nodes cache the base once and pull only the adapters (see Getting model weights into pods).
  • Watch the rank and count limits: max-loras and max-lora-rank reserve GPU memory, which comes out of the KV cache.

Running tuning jobs with Kubeflow Trainer

Scenario. Data scientists submit fine-tuning jobs by SSHing into a GPU box and running torchrun by hand. Jobs collide, nobody knows who's using which GPU, and a crashed run is just lost. The platform team wants jobs submitted from Python, with GPUs, networking and checkpoints handled by the platform.

What the picture shows. Who owns what, and what runs.

1The platform team defines TrainingRuntimes
(or cluster-wide ClusterTrainingRuntimes) for PyTorch, DeepSpeed, MLX and MPI: images, network settings, node placement, how the distributed environment is set up.
2Data scientists submit TrainJobs
from Python with the Kubeflow SDK. Their training function is serialized into the job, so there's no image rebuild per experiment.
3The controller turns each TrainJob into a JobSet,
with one pod per node and the distributed environment (ranks, master address) set up for torchrun.
4Kueue admits the whole job or none of it,
so a 4-node job never starts with 3 nodes. See Gang scheduling and Queueing and fair sharing.
5Checkpoints go to persistent storage,
so a preempted or failed job resumes instead of starting over.

The code. The same job from the Python SDK, and as YAML.

from kubeflow.trainer import TrainerClient, CustomTrainer def fine_tune():    # runs on every node under torchrun; imports inside the function    import torch.distributed as dist    from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer    ...                                   # the LoRA code from the previous section client = TrainerClient()job = client.train(    runtime=client.get_runtime("torch-distributed"),     # defined by the platform team    trainer=CustomTrainer(        func=fine_tune,                                  # serialized into the job, no image build        num_nodes=2,        resources_per_node={"gpu": 4, "cpu": 32, "memory": "256Gi"},        packages_to_install=["trl", "peft"],    ),)client.wait_for_job_status(job)for line in client.get_job_logs(job, follow=True):    print(line)
apiVersion: trainer.kubeflow.org/v1alpha1kind: TrainJobmetadata:  name: support-tone-lora  namespace: team-support  labels:    kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: training          # all-or-nothing admissionspec:  runtimeRef:    name: torch-distributed  trainer:    image: registry.example.com/train/sft:2026.11    numNodes: 2    resourcesPerNode:      limits: { nvidia.com/gpu: 4 }    command: ["torchrun", "train.py", "--resume-from", "latest"]
Going deeper2 points
  • The runtime is where platform expertise lives: EFA and NCCL settings, shared memory, the checkpoint path and metrics are defined once and tested, not copied into every job. See Kubeflow Trainer.
  • Alternatives: Ray/KubeRay (RayJob on a RayCluster; code ships in images or repositories), DeepSpeed as a training library inside any of these, and Unsloth for fast single-GPU fine-tuning.

Data, network and checkpoints

Scenario. A 2-node fine-tune runs at half the expected speed. The GPUs aren't the bottleneck: sharded training moves weights between nodes on every layer, and the pods are talking over the ordinary pod network instead of the fast interconnect.

What the picture shows. The three data paths of a multi-node tuning job.

1Data in
the dataset and base model are loaded at startup, ideally from storage in the same region (S3, FSx or a model image). An initializer step can download them once for all nodes.
2GPU to GPU
sharded training (PyTorch FSDP2) gathers and scatters weights between GPUs on every layer. Inside a node that's NVLink; between nodes it needs a fast network (EFA on AWS), or the network becomes the bottleneck.
3Checkpoints out
saved every N steps to a PersistentVolume or object storage, so a restart resumes from the last one.
4The result
the final adapter or model goes to the model registry with its training metadata.

The YAML. A checkpoint volume shared by the job's pods (in the TrainJob's pod template overrides or the runtime).

apiVersion: v1kind: PersistentVolumeClaimmetadata:  name: support-tone-checkpoints  namespace: team-supportspec:  accessModes: ["ReadWriteMany"]              # every rank writes its shard  storageClassName: fsx-lustre  resources: { requests: { storage: 200Gi } }
Going deeper2 points
  • Rank 0 often writes everything in simple training scripts. For larger jobs, use sharded checkpoints so every rank writes its own part in parallel.
  • Clean up: checkpoints of finished experiments add up fast. Keep the final one and the best one, and expire the rest.
Further research

RAG and agents on Kubernetes

  1. Two application shapes
  2. RAG ingestion: from documents to vectors
  3. RAG at query time
  4. Mapping RAG onto Kubernetes
  5. Agents

In a real product, the model is one service among many. The application owns the logic: it fetches context, calls tools, keeps state, and uses the LLM for generation and reasoning. This post maps those pieces onto Kubernetes: the two application shapes, a RAG pipeline from ingestion to answer, the Kubernetes objects behind it, and agents.

Two application shapes

Scenario. A team builds a chat assistant and a nightly job that summarizes support tickets on the same stack: always-on Deployments behind a load balancer. The chat app is fine. The summarizer sits idle 23 hours a day on reserved GPUs, then overwhelms the model at midnight when 40,000 tickets arrive at once.

What the picture shows. Two shapes of AI application, with different priorities.

1Chat apps
gateway → orchestrator → LLM → state store, all within one synchronous request. Latency rules, so everything stays warm, and browser-based sign-in (OAuth2) is easy.
2Backend AI services
triggered by events (an order placed, a payment made) or by a schedule. They need idempotency, buffering and eventual consistency more than raw speed, and can scale to zero between bursts.
3A queue between events and the model
absorbs bursts: workers pull at the rate the model can serve, instead of the event source pushing as fast as it can.
4Around these sit
nightly CronJobs, always-on agent loops (single-replica Deployments that watch a feed, like a controller with an LLM inside), and multi-step automations that run as Jobs.

The YAML. An event-driven worker that scales from zero on a Kafka topic's backlog with KEDA.

apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1kind: ScaledObjectmetadata:  name: ticket-summarizer  namespace: support-aispec:  scaleTargetRef: { name: ticket-summarizer }     # a Deployment of workers  minReplicaCount: 0                              # nothing runs when there's no work  maxReplicaCount: 20                             # caps load on the shared model  triggers:  - type: kafka    metadata:      bootstrapServers: kafka.data.svc:9092      consumerGroup: ticket-summarizer      topic: tickets.created      lagThreshold: "50"                          # ~50 waiting tickets per worker
Going deeper2 points
  • Cap the workers, not just the model: maxReplicaCount on the workers is what protects the shared model from a burst. See Thundering herd.
  • Make every step idempotent: events get redelivered, so a worker must recognize a ticket it already summarized. See Workloads and node tiers.

RAG ingestion: from documents to vectors

Scenario. The assistant answers questions about internal policies, but its answers are three months out of date, because someone ran the indexing script once from a laptop. Ingestion needs to be a scheduled, repeatable pipeline with an owner.

What the picture shows. The offline half of RAG, run as Jobs or CronJobs.

1Parse
turn PDFs, HTML and office files into clean text with structure (headings, tables), for example with Docling.
2Chunk
split into pieces by sentence, paragraph or heading, small enough to be specific and large enough to make sense on their own, often with some overlap.
3Embed
turn each chunk into a vector with an embedding model, served like any other model.
4Upsert
write the vectors with metadata (source, section, version, access group) into a vector database. Upsert by a stable ID, so re-running the job updates instead of duplicating.
5Only what changed
the job processes documents modified since its last run, which keeps nightly runs small.

The code and YAML. The heart of the ingestion job, and the CronJob that runs it with limits so it can't starve user traffic.

import hashlibfrom openai import OpenAIfrom qdrant_client import QdrantClientfrom qdrant_client.models import PointStruct embedder = OpenAI(base_url="http://embedder.rag.svc:8000/v1", api_key="unused")db = QdrantClient(url="http://qdrant.rag.svc:6333") def chunks(text: str, size: int = 800, overlap: int = 100):    for start in range(0, len(text), size - overlap):        yield text[start:start + size] def ingest(doc_id: str, text: str, meta: dict) -> None:    parts = list(chunks(text))    vectors = embedder.embeddings.create(model="bge-m3", input=parts).data    db.upsert("policies", points=[        PointStruct(            id=int(hashlib.sha1(f"{doc_id}:{i}".encode()).hexdigest()[:15], 16),  # stable ID            vector=v.embedding,            payload={**meta, "doc_id": doc_id, "chunk": i, "text": part},        )        for i, (part, v) in enumerate(zip(parts, vectors))    ])
apiVersion: batch/v1kind: CronJobmetadata:  name: ingest-policies  namespace: ragspec:  schedule: "0 2 * * *"  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid                      # never two runs at once  jobTemplate:    spec:      backoffLimit: 2      template:        spec:          restartPolicy: OnFailure          priorityClassName: batch-low           # users' requests come first          containers:          - name: ingest            image: registry.example.com/rag/ingest:1.8            args: ["--source", "s3://docs/policies/", "--since-last-run"]            resources:              requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 2Gi }              limits:   { cpu: "2", memory: 4Gi }
Going deeper2 points
  • Changing the embedding model means re-embedding every document, because vectors from different models can't be compared. Version the collection (policies-bge-m3-v2) and switch over when it's complete.
  • Store access groups in the metadata and filter on them at query time, so users only retrieve chunks they're allowed to read.

RAG at query time

Scenario. Users complain that the assistant confidently cites a policy that doesn't say what it claims. The retrieval found the right document, but the prompt didn't ask the model to stick to it, and nothing checked the answer before it went out.

What the picture shows. The online half of RAG, inside one request.

1Embed the question
with the same embedding model used at ingestion.
2Search
a similarity search for the closest chunks, optionally hybrid with keyword ranking (better for names, codes and exact terms), filtered by the user's access groups.
3Rerank (optional)
a reranker model reorders the top 20–50 chunks by relevance, for high-stakes questions.
4Build the prompt
from a versioned template: instructions, the selected chunks with their sources, the question.
5Generate,
then add citations and run output guardrails before returning the answer.

The code. The query path, end to end.

from openai import OpenAIfrom qdrant_client import QdrantClientfrom qdrant_client.models import FieldCondition, Filter, MatchAny llm = OpenAI(base_url="http://qwen-7b.models.svc:8000/v1", api_key="unused")embedder = OpenAI(base_url="http://embedder.rag.svc:8000/v1", api_key="unused")db = QdrantClient(url="http://qdrant.rag.svc:6333") PROMPT = """Answer only from the sources below. If they don't contain the answer, say so.Cite sources as [n].\n\n{sources}\n\nQuestion: {question}""" def answer(question: str, user_groups: list[str]) -> str:    qvec = embedder.embeddings.create(model="bge-m3", input=[question]).data[0].embedding  # same model    hits = db.query_points(        "policies", query=qvec, limit=6,        query_filter=Filter(must=[FieldCondition(key="access_group", match=MatchAny(any=user_groups))]),    ).points    sources = "\n".join(f"[{i+1}] ({h.payload['doc_id']}) {h.payload['text']}" for i, h in enumerate(hits))    reply = llm.chat.completions.create(        model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct",        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": PROMPT.format(sources=sources, question=question)}],        temperature=0.1,    )    return reply.choices[0].message.content      # then: citations check, output guardrails
Going deeper2 points
  • Measure retrieval separately from generation. If the right chunk isn't in the top results, no prompt will fix the answer. Ragas-style metrics (context relevance, faithfulness) separate the two; see Running LLMs in production.
  • Prompts are configuration: keep the template in a ConfigMap or a prompt registry, versioned with the deployment, so a prompt change is reviewed and reversible.

Mapping RAG onto Kubernetes

Scenario. The RAG prototype runs as one container with an embedded vector store. To go to production, the team needs to decide which piece is a Deployment, which is stateful, and how they're protected from each other.

What the picture shows. Each RAG component and the Kubernetes shape it takes.

Component Kubernetes shape
Vector DB (Milvus, Weaviate, Qdrant, pgvector) StatefulSet + PVC, snapshots, NetworkPolicy
Embedding model Deployment, sidecar, or in-process
Orchestrator Deployment + Service/Ingress; prompts in ConfigMaps, keys in Secrets
Reranker Optional Deployment for high-stakes queries
Ingestion CronJob / Job with limits so it can't starve users

The YAML. The vector database as a StatefulSet, reachable only from the orchestrator and the ingestion job.

apiVersion: apps/v1kind: StatefulSetmetadata:  name: qdrant  namespace: ragspec:  serviceName: qdrant  replicas: 3  selector: { matchLabels: { app: qdrant } }  template:    metadata:      labels: { app: qdrant }    spec:      containers:      - name: qdrant        image: qdrant/qdrant:v1.15.0        ports: [ { containerPort: 6333, name: http } ]        resources:          requests: { cpu: "2", memory: 8Gi }        volumeMounts: [ { name: data, mountPath: /qdrant/storage } ]  volumeClaimTemplates:                          # one volume per replica  - metadata: { name: data }    spec:      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]      storageClassName: gp3      resources: { requests: { storage: 100Gi } }---apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1kind: NetworkPolicymetadata:  name: qdrant-clients-only  namespace: ragspec:  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: qdrant } }  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]  ingress:  - from:    - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: rag-orchestrator } }   # reads    - podSelector: { matchLabels: { job: ingest-policies } }    # writes    ports: [ { port: 6333 } ]
Going deeper2 points
  • The vector store holds your documents in plain text (the chunk payloads). Protect it like the source systems: network policy, encryption at rest, backups and snapshots, and access groups in the metadata.
  • See Workloads, node groups and scheduling for where stateful AI components should run.

Agents

Scenario. The support team wants the assistant to do more than answer: look up the customer's order, check the refund policy, and draft the refund, asking a human before it sends money. That's no longer a single prompt and answer; it's a loop with tools.

What the picture shows. The agent loop, and where its pieces run on Kubernetes.

1The loop
perceive → think → act (call a tool) → observe the result → reflect → remember, repeated until the task is done. ReAct is the classic form.
2Tools
run either on the client (the model asks your code to run a function) or on the server, increasingly through MCP servers. See Running agents in production.
3Frameworks
client-side libraries (LangChain, LangGraph, CrewAI) or server-side runtimes behind an API (OpenAI-style Responses API, Llama Stack, vLLM's emerging support). Server-side runtimes handle state and human approval steps for you.
4On Kubernetes
agents are Deployments, tools are Services, memory lives in StatefulSets, and heavy work goes to Jobs. Operators like Kagent declare agents, tools and A2A skills as custom resources.
5Human approval for risky actions
the loop pauses before tools that send money, delete data or message customers, and continues only when a person approves.

The YAML. A Kagent agent declared as a custom resource, with its model and an MCP tool server.

apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2kind: ModelConfigmetadata:  name: in-cluster-qwen  namespace: kagentspec:  provider: OpenAI                                # any OpenAI-compatible endpoint  model: Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct  apiKeySecret: llm-api-key  apiKeySecretKey: key  openAI:    baseUrl: http://qwen-7b.models.svc:8000/v1---apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha2kind: Agentmetadata:  name: refund-assistant  namespace: kagentspec:  description: Looks up orders and drafts refunds within policy.  type: Declarative  declarative:    modelConfig: in-cluster-qwen    systemMessage: |      You help support agents with refunds. Look up the order, check the refund policy,      and draft the refund. Never issue a refund yourself; a person approves it.    tools:    - type: McpServer      mcpServer:        apiGroup: kagent.dev        kind: RemoteMCPServer        name: orders-mcp                          # read-only order lookup        toolNames: ["get_order", "get_refund_policy", "draft_refund"]
Going deeper3 points
  • Multi-agent systems use either a coordinator agent that delegates to specialists, or peer-to-peer messaging, plus shared memory. Plan for failures between steps (sagas: each step has an undo) and require human approval for risky actions.
  • Give agents the fewest tools that do the job. A short tool list is both safer (less for a prompt injection to reach) and more accurate (models choose worse from long lists).
  • Untrusted code from agents belongs in a sandbox; see Design 01. Long-running agents need durable state; see Design 04.
Further research

Running agents in production

  1. MCP: one protocol for tools
  2. Whose identity reaches the backend?
  3. Combining identities: workload, user and policy
  4. MCP gateways
  5. A2A: agents talking to agents
  6. Memory and long-running work

Agents bring three problems that plain microservices don't: who they act as, how they talk to tools and to each other, and what they remember. The protocols are still young, but the operational patterns below hold regardless of framework: MCP for tools, a deliberate choice of identity, gateways in front of tools, A2A between agents, and memory that survives restarts.

MCP: one protocol for tools

Scenario. Four agent teams each wrote their own integration with the same six internal systems: 24 integrations, each with its own auth, error handling and bugs. When the orders API changed, five of them broke.

What the picture shows. Why a common tool protocol changes the maths.

1Without a protocol
every agent integrates with every tool, so M agents and N tools mean M×N integrations.
2With MCP (Model Context Protocol)
each tool is wrapped once as an MCP server, and every agent speaks MCP, so it's M+N.
3Tools describe themselves
a name, a description and a JSON schema for the arguments. The agent's model reads the descriptions to decide which tool to call.
4Calls use JSON-RPC
over a transport; for servers on Kubernetes that's streamable HTTP.
5Governance
MCP now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, together with goose and AGENTS.md.

The code and YAML. An MCP server in Python that exposes two read-only tools, and how it runs on Kubernetes.

# orders_mcp.pyfrom mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCPimport httpx mcp = FastMCP("orders", host="0.0.0.0", port=8000, stateless_http=True)   # no session state in the pod @mcp.tool()def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict:    """Look up an order by ID: items, status, amount and customer ID."""    return httpx.get(f"http://orders-api.shop.svc/orders/{order_id}", timeout=5).json() @mcp.tool()def get_refund_policy(country: str) -> str:    """Return the refund policy text for a country code such as 'DE' or 'US'."""    return httpx.get(f"http://policy-api.shop.svc/refunds/{country}", timeout=5).text if __name__ == "__main__":    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")
apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: orders-mcp  namespace: mcpspec:  replicas: 2  selector: { matchLabels: { app: orders-mcp } }  template:    metadata:      labels: { app: orders-mcp, mcp.example.com/server: "true" }    spec:      serviceAccountName: orders-mcp          # its own identity toward the orders API      containers:      - name: server        image: registry.example.com/mcp/orders:1.3        ports: [ { containerPort: 8000, name: mcp } ]        readinessProbe: { tcpSocket: { port: mcp } }        resources: { requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi } }---apiVersion: v1kind: Servicemetadata:  name: orders-mcp  namespace: mcpspec:  selector: { app: orders-mcp }  ports: [ { port: 80, targetPort: mcp } ]     # agents connect to http://orders-mcp.mcp/mcp
Going deeper3 points
  • Run each MCP server as a Deployment behind a Service, keep session state outside the pod (or run stateless, as above), and scale with an HPA like any API.
  • Use a sidecar only when the tool must share the agent's files (a code-editing tool working on the agent's workspace, for example).
  • Group related tools into one server to keep the number of services manageable, and watch the total tool count per agent, because models choose less well from very long lists.

Whose identity reaches the backend?

Scenario. A support agent calls the orders API on behalf of a user. The orders API's audit log shows every call coming from "refund-assistant", so nobody can tell which user's request triggered a refund, and the agent can read every customer's orders, not just the ones the user is allowed to see.

What the picture shows. Four ways to carry identity from a user, through an agent, to a backend.

1Token passthrough
the agent forwards the user's OAuth token. Existing per-user permissions and audit just work, but tokens expire during long tasks, scopes are usually too broad, and a stolen token works anywhere.
2ServiceAccount delegation
the agent uses its pod's ServiceAccount token; backends validate it with TokenReview and authorize with SubjectAccessReview on app-specific "virtual" resources. No extra identity provider, but only the workload is visible, not the user.
3Token exchange (RFC 8693)
the identity provider issues a new token with the user in sub and the agent in act. Backends see both and can apply composite policies ("support users, through the refund agent, may read orders").
4SPIFFE/SPIRE mTLS
SPIRE issues short-lived X.509 identities per pod through a node agent. No secrets to steal, and automatic rotation, at the cost of significant setup and operations.
Pattern Strength Watch out for
Token passthrough Existing per-user RBAC and audit just work Token expiry on long tasks, broad scopes, stolen tokens
ServiceAccount delegation No extra identity provider inside the cluster Workload identity only, no user
Token exchange (RFC 8693) User and agent visible; composite policies Run and cache an exchange service
SPIFFE/SPIRE mTLS No secrets to steal; auto-rotation Significant setup and operations

The code. A token exchange: the agent trades the user's token, plus its own identity, for a narrow token for one backend.

import httpx def exchange_for_orders_api(user_token: str, agent_token: str) -> str:    resp = httpx.post(        "https://idp.example.com/oauth2/token",        data={            "grant_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange",            "subject_token": user_token,                  # who the request is for → sub            "subject_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token",            "actor_token": agent_token,                   # who is acting → act            "actor_token_type": "urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:jwt",            "audience": "orders-api",                     # only valid for this backend            "scope": "orders:read",                       # narrower than the user's token        },        timeout=5,    )    resp.raise_for_status()    return resp.json()["access_token"]                    # short-lived; cache until expiry
Going deeper2 points
  • The exchanged token is narrower than the original: one audience, fewer scopes, shorter lifetime. That's what limits the damage if an agent is tricked into misusing it.
  • See Identity and model endpoints for workload identity and guardrails on the model side.

Combining identities: workload, user and policy

Scenario. Security asks for one rule: "only the refund agent, acting for a user in the support group, may call draft_refund". No single identity pattern can express that; it needs the workload's identity, the user's identity and a policy that checks both.

What the picture shows. How production setups combine the patterns.

1Workload identity through SPIFFE mTLS
the connection itself proves that the caller is the refund-assistant workload; no secret in the pod.
2User identity in a header or an exchanged token
the request carries who it's for.
3A policy engine (OPA) checks both
the tool server, or the gateway in front of it, asks "may this workload, acting for this user, call this tool?".
4Every decision is logged
with the workload, the user, the tool and the outcome.

The YAML and policy. SPIRE issues an identity per ServiceAccount; OPA requires both identities.

apiVersion: spire.spiffe.io/v1alpha1kind: ClusterSPIFFEIDmetadata:  name: agentsspec:  spiffeIDTemplate: "spiffe://{{ .TrustDomain }}/ns/{{ .PodMeta.Namespace }}/sa/{{ .PodSpec.ServiceAccountName }}"  namespaceSelector:    matchLabels: { workload-class: agents }      # every agent pod gets a short-lived identity
package mcp.authz default allow := false allow if {    input.workload == "spiffe://example.org/ns/agents/sa/refund-assistant"   # who is calling    "support" in input.user.groups                                          # for whom    input.tool in {"get_order", "get_refund_policy", "draft_refund"}}
Going deeper2 points
  • Start with the simplest pattern that answers your audit question, usually token exchange, and add SPIFFE when you have many workloads and want to remove static credentials.
  • Policies are code: keep them in Git, test them with example inputs in CI, and roll them out like any other change.

MCP gateways

Scenario. Twenty MCP servers each implement their own authentication, rate limits and logging, in three languages and with different bugs. The security team can't answer "which agent called which tool for whom yesterday?" without reading twenty log formats.

What the picture shows. A gateway that every agent goes through to reach tools.

1One entry point for tools
agents connect to the gateway; the gateway connects to the MCP servers.
2Authentication and authorization in one place
the gateway validates the agent's and user's identity and applies tool-level policy before a call reaches the server.
3Rate limits and quotas
per agent, per user and per tool.
4Audit
one log of every tool call, with the same fields for every server.
5Tool filtering
the gateway can expose only the tools a given agent is allowed to use, so the model never even sees the others.
6Examples
Envoy AI Gateway, agentgateway, ContextForge and others.

The YAML. Make the gateway the only way in: MCP servers accept traffic only from the gateway's pods.

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1kind: NetworkPolicymetadata:  name: mcp-servers-gateway-only  namespace: mcpspec:  podSelector:    matchLabels: { mcp.example.com/server: "true" }   # every MCP server  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]  ingress:  - from:    - namespaceSelector:        matchLabels: { kubernetes.io/metadata.name: mcp-gateway }      podSelector:        matchLabels: { app: mcp-gateway }             # agents can't bypass it    ports: [ { port: 8000 } ]
Going deeper2 points
  • The gateway is an extra hop that must be highly available: run several replicas across zones with a PodDisruptionBudget, because every agent's tool calls depend on it.
  • Start without one if you have a handful of tool servers; add a gateway when the number of servers, agents or audit requirements makes per-server controls unmanageable.

A2A: agents talking to agents

Scenario. A travel-booking agent needs a flight agent and a hotel agent, built by different teams, possibly in different frameworks. A booking can take minutes and may need the user's input halfway through. A tool call that returns in one HTTP response doesn't fit.

What the picture shows. MCP connects an agent to tools; the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol connects an agent to other agents, which can reason and take time.

1An agent card
advertises the agent's skills, input and output formats, endpoint and capabilities, like an OpenAPI spec. It's served at a well-known path, so other agents can discover it.
2A task lifecycle
that outlives any single HTTP call: submitted → working, possibly pausing at input-required, then completed, failed or canceled.
3Streamed artifacts
deliver partial results (an itinerary draft, then the confirmed booking) while the task is still running.
4On Kubernetes
each agent is its own Deployment, with NetworkPolicies between them and circuit breakers in the mesh, so one slow agent doesn't take down the others.

The code. An agent card for the flight agent (JSON).

{  "name": "flight-agent",  "description": "Searches and books flights within the company travel policy.",  "url": "https://flight-agent.agents.example.com/a2a",  "version": "1.4.0",  "capabilities": { "streaming": true, "pushNotifications": true },  "defaultInputModes": ["text/plain", "application/json"],  "defaultOutputModes": ["application/json"],  "skills": [    {      "id": "search-flights",      "name": "Search flights",      "description": "Find flights between two airports on given dates, within policy.",      "tags": ["travel", "flights"]    },    {      "id": "book-flight",      "name": "Book a flight",      "description": "Book a selected flight. Asks for traveller confirmation before payment.",      "tags": ["travel", "booking"]    }  ]}
Going deeper2 points
  • Treat the agent card as a contract you check in CI: a change to a skill's name or input format breaks the agents that call it, just like an API change.
  • Alert on tasks stuck in working: a task that never finishes holds resources and leaves a user waiting. Track task duration and state counts as metrics.

Memory and long-running work

Scenario. The refund agent works fine until the Deployment scales from one replica to three. Now users' second messages land on a replica that doesn't remember the first, and an agent that was halfway through a 20-minute investigation starts over when its pod is evicted.

What the picture shows. Where each kind of agent memory belongs.

1In-memory state
is fine for development and lost on the first restart or scale-out.
2Short-term memory (the session)
belongs in a key-value store such as Redis, run as a StatefulSet, with a TTL per session, so any replica can serve the next turn.
3Long-term memory
(preferences, audit trail, cross-session analytics) belongs in a database, written asynchronously so it doesn't slow the conversation.
4Long-running agents
checkpoint after each major step to durable storage and run as Jobs with restartPolicy: OnFailure, so an evicted pod resumes where it left off. The checkpoints double as a debugging trail.

The code and YAML. Session memory in Redis, and a long-running agent as a Job that resumes from its checkpoint.

import jsonimport redis r = redis.Redis(host="redis.agents.svc", port=6379, decode_responses=True)SESSION_TTL = 60 * 60 * 24                                 # sessions expire after a day def load_history(session_id: str) -> list[dict]:    return [json.loads(m) for m in r.lrange(f"session:{session_id}", 0, -1)] def append_turn(session_id: str, role: str, content: str) -> None:    key = f"session:{session_id}"    r.rpush(key, json.dumps({"role": role, "content": content}))    r.expire(key, SESSION_TTL)                             # any replica can serve the next turn
apiVersion: batch/v1kind: Jobmetadata:  name: investigate-incident-4821  namespace: agentsspec:  backoffLimit: 5  template:    spec:      restartPolicy: OnFailure                             # an evicted pod comes back...      containers:      - name: agent        image: registry.example.com/agents/investigator:2.1        args: ["--task-id", "4821", "--checkpoint-dir", "/state"]   # ...and resumes from here        volumeMounts: [ { name: state, mountPath: /state } ]      volumes:      - name: state        persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: investigator-state }
Going deeper2 points
  • For agents that run for hours or days, checkpoints on a volume aren't enough: you also need to avoid repeating side effects and to wait cheaply for people. Design 04 covers a durable execution design for that.
  • Start with plain Deployments, Services, RBAC and StatefulSets, and add meshes, gateways and operators only when a real limitation shows up.
Appendix

Appendix A: Running a second scheduler on a managed cluster

  1. When you need a second scheduler
  2. How two schedulers share one cluster
  3. Step 1: identity and permissions
  4. Step 2: the scheduler's configuration
  5. Step 3: run the scheduler
  6. Step 4: opt workloads in
  7. Giving it its own nodes
  8. Autoscaling with a second scheduler
  9. Checking that it works, and troubleshooting
  10. Operating it over time

This appendix is a complete, ready-to-apply guide for one specific situation: you want different scheduling rules for some of your workloads (different plugin weights, or bin-packing instead of spreading), but you're on a managed cluster such as EKS, GKE or AKS, where you can't change the default scheduler's configuration.

The answer is to run a second scheduler next to the default one. It's the same official kube-scheduler program, deployed by you as an ordinary Deployment, with its own KubeSchedulerConfiguration. Pods choose it by setting schedulerName; every other pod keeps using the default scheduler. For background, see Phase 1: filtering (the note on KubeSchedulerConfiguration), Phase 2: scoring plugins and Built-in plugins, and what a second scheduler changes.

When you need a second scheduler

Scenario. A platform team runs batch jobs and web services on the same EKS cluster. Batch pods are spread evenly across nodes, so dozens of nodes stay 30% full and Karpenter can never remove them. The team wants batch pods packed tightly, but EKS doesn't let anyone change the managed scheduler's scoring. Before deploying anything, they need to know whether a second scheduler is really the right tool.

What the picture shows. A decision path from "I want different placement" to the lightest tool that achieves it.

1Can the pod say it itself?
Node affinity, pod affinity and anti-affinity, topology spread constraints, taints and tolerations change where one workload goes, with no new components. Try these first. See Phase 1: filtering.
2Do you need to change the scoring itself?
Plugin weights, bin-packing (MostAllocated) instead of spreading, or turning a plugin off can't be expressed in a pod spec. Only a scheduler configuration can do it, and on a managed cluster the only configuration you control is your own scheduler's.
3Is the problem really about jobs, not pods?
All-or-nothing starts, quotas between teams and queueing are job-level problems. Use Kueue, Volcano or KAI (see Volcano vs. Kueue), not a second kube-scheduler.
4Do you only need bin-packing for node cost?
On EKS, Karpenter consolidation already repacks nodes after the fact. A second scheduler packs at placement time, so nodes empty out sooner, but it's one more component to run.
5The answer for the scenario
batch needs different scoring, and only for batch pods, so a second scheduler with a bin-packing profile is the right tool.
Going deeper2 points
  • A second scheduler is still kube-scheduler. Same filters, same plugins, same API fields; only the configuration differs. That's why it's far less risky than writing a custom scheduler from scratch.
  • Profiles versus schedulers: on a self-managed cluster you'd add a second profile to the default scheduler instead. On a managed cluster you can't, so you run your own kube-scheduler process that holds one or more profiles of its own.

How two schedulers share one cluster

Scenario. Before deploying, the team wants to understand what happens when two schedulers watch the same pods and nodes. Who decides which scheduler handles a pod, and what stops them from fighting over it?

What the picture shows. Two independent scheduler processes, one API server, and the field that splits the work between them.

1spec.schedulerName routes the pod
every pod has it; when it's unset, the API server fills in default-scheduler. Each scheduler only picks up pods whose schedulerName matches one of its profiles and ignores the rest.
2Both read the same cluster state
each scheduler keeps its own cache of nodes and pods, built from watches on the API server. Neither knows the other exists.
3Binding is the only write
a scheduler's decision is a Binding that sets the pod's nodeName. After that, the kubelet on that node runs the pod.
4Leader election per scheduler
each scheduler runs two replicas and uses its own Lease object, so only one replica of each is active. The default scheduler's lease and yours never collide because the names differ.
5The kubelet is the referee
if both schedulers place pods on the same node at the same moment and together they don't fit, the kubelet rejects the pod that arrives second (an admission failure such as OutOfcpu). The rejected pod is marked as failed, and its controller replaces it.
Going deeper2 points
  • The race is rare but real. Each scheduler assumes its own placements immediately, but only learns about the other scheduler's placements through watch events a moment later. It matters most on full nodes, which is exactly where a bin-packing scheduler aims. That's why the guide gives the second scheduler its own nodes (see Giving it its own nodes).
  • schedulerName can't be changed after a pod is created. Moving a workload between schedulers means changing its pod template, which rolls out new pods.

Step 1: identity and permissions

Scenario. The first attempt at deploying the scheduler starts fine, but neither replica ever becomes the leader, and the logs fill with "leases.coordination.k8s.io is forbidden". The built-in scheduler role was written for the default scheduler, and it doesn't cover a lease with a different name.

What the YAML does.

  • A ServiceAccount, my-scheduler, in kube-system, used by the scheduler's pods.
  • Reuses the built-in roles: bound to system:kube-scheduler (read pods and nodes, create bindings, update pod status) and system:volume-scheduler (needed for pods with PersistentVolumeClaims), so you don't maintain your own copy of the scheduler's permissions.
  • Reads the API server's authentication settings: the extension-apiserver-authentication-reader Role, so the scheduler's own HTTPS endpoint can authenticate requests to /metrics.
  • Adds the lease permission the built-in role lacks: system:kube-scheduler lets the default scheduler update only the lease named kube-scheduler. A small extra Role lets your scheduler get and update its own lease, affinity-first-scheduler. Without it, leader election fails and nothing gets scheduled.
apiVersion: v1kind: ServiceAccountmetadata:  name: my-scheduler  namespace: kube-system---apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1kind: ClusterRoleBindingmetadata:  name: my-scheduler-as-kube-schedulersubjects:- { kind: ServiceAccount, name: my-scheduler, namespace: kube-system }roleRef:  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io  kind: ClusterRole  name: system:kube-scheduler        # read pods/nodes, bind pods---apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1kind: ClusterRoleBindingmetadata:  name: my-scheduler-as-volume-schedulersubjects:- { kind: ServiceAccount, name: my-scheduler, namespace: kube-system }roleRef:  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io  kind: ClusterRole  name: system:volume-scheduler      # needed for pods with PVCs---apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1kind: RoleBindingmetadata:  name: my-scheduler-auth-reader  namespace: kube-systemsubjects:- { kind: ServiceAccount, name: my-scheduler, namespace: kube-system }roleRef:  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io  kind: Role  name: extension-apiserver-authentication-reader---# The built-in role only covers the lease named "kube-scheduler"apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1kind: Rolemetadata:  name: my-scheduler-lease  namespace: kube-systemrules:- apiGroups: ["coordination.k8s.io"]  resources: ["leases"]  verbs: ["create"]- apiGroups: ["coordination.k8s.io"]  resources: ["leases"]  resourceNames: ["affinity-first-scheduler"]   # must match leaderElection.resourceName  verbs: ["get", "update"]---apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1kind: RoleBindingmetadata:  name: my-scheduler-lease  namespace: kube-systemsubjects:- { kind: ServiceAccount, name: my-scheduler, namespace: kube-system }roleRef:  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io  kind: Role  name: my-scheduler-lease
Going deeper2 points
  • Don't edit the built-in ClusterRole. Some guides add your scheduler's name to system:kube-scheduler itself. On a managed cluster that role is owned by the provider and can be reset on upgrade; a separate Role survives upgrades.
  • Least privilege still applies. The scheduler can bind any pod in the cluster to any node. Treat its ServiceAccount, its namespace and its image as part of the control plane: restrict who can change them.

Step 2: the scheduler's configuration

Scenario. The team's batch nodes are 32-CPU machines. With the default spreading behaviour, 40 batch pods of 4 CPUs each land on 20 nodes at 25% each. Packed tightly, the same pods need 5 nodes, and Karpenter can remove the rest.

What the picture shows. The same pods placed by two scoring strategies, and the configuration that changes one into the other.

1LeastAllocated (the default)
NodeResourcesFit scores emptier nodes higher, so pods spread out. Good for availability, bad for node cost.
2MostAllocated (bin-packing)
the same plugin scores fuller nodes higher, so pods fill one node before the next. Empty nodes can be removed by the autoscaler.
3Resource weights
the resources list decides which resources count when measuring "full". For GPU clusters, add nvidia.com/gpu with a high weight so GPU nodes fill first.
4Plugin weights
the profile also raises InterPodAffinity to 100 (pods that want to be together win over everything else) and lowers ImageLocality to 1.
5Leader election
on, with its own lease name, so two replicas can run safely.
apiVersion: v1kind: ConfigMapmetadata:  name: my-scheduler-config  namespace: kube-systemdata:  config.yaml: |    apiVersion: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1    kind: KubeSchedulerConfiguration    leaderElection:      leaderElect: true                # 2 replicas, only one active      resourceNamespace: kube-system      resourceName: affinity-first-scheduler    profiles:    - schedulerName: affinity-first-scheduler      plugins:        score:          enabled:          - name: InterPodAffinity            weight: 100          - name: ImageLocality            weight: 1      pluginConfig:      - name: NodeResourcesFit        args:          scoringStrategy:            type: MostAllocated        # bin-pack instead of spread            resources:            - name: cpu              weight: 1            - name: memory              weight: 1
Going deeper4 points
  • One process, several profiles. A single scheduler Deployment can hold more than one profile, each with its own schedulerName, for example a CPU bin-packing profile and a GPU bin-packing profile. They share one cache and one leader election, which is cheaper than running two Deployments.
    profiles:    - schedulerName: binpack-cpu      pluginConfig:      - name: NodeResourcesFit        args:          scoringStrategy:            type: MostAllocated            resources: [ { name: cpu, weight: 1 }, { name: memory, weight: 1 } ]    - schedulerName: binpack-gpu      pluginConfig:      - name: NodeResourcesFit        args:          scoringStrategy:            type: MostAllocated            resources:            - { name: nvidia.com/gpu, weight: 10 }   # fill GPU nodes first            - { name: cpu, weight: 1 }            - { name: memory, weight: 1 }
  • RequestedToCapacityRatio is the third scoring strategy: you draw a curve of score against utilization, for example "best at 80% full, worse above 95%", if pure bin-packing leaves no headroom.
  • Bin-packing has a cost: more pods per node means a bigger blast radius when a node fails. Keep it for batch and other interruption-tolerant work, and leave latency-sensitive services on the default scheduler.
  • percentageOfNodesToScore limits how many feasible nodes are scored on very large clusters. Leave the default unless scheduling latency is a measured problem.

Step 3: run the scheduler

Scenario. The scheduler is now part of the control plane for every batch pod. If it goes down, batch pods sit in Pending with no explanation. It needs to be run like the control-plane component it is.

What the YAML does.

  • Two replicas, spread across zones: leader election keeps only one active; the other takes over within seconds if the leader fails. Topology spread puts them in different zones.
  • High priority: system-cluster-critical, so the scheduler is never evicted to make room for the pods it's supposed to place.
  • The official image, pinned to your cluster's version: registry.k8s.io/kube-scheduler with --config pointing at the mounted ConfigMap.
  • Health checks on the secure port (10259): the liveness probe restarts a hung scheduler.
  • A PodDisruptionBudget: node drains and Karpenter consolidation can never take both replicas down at once.
  • Runs on nodes it doesn't schedule onto: the scheduler itself is placed by the default scheduler on system nodes, so it doesn't depend on itself to start.
apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: my-scheduler  namespace: kube-systemspec:  replicas: 2  selector:    matchLabels: { component: my-scheduler }  template:    metadata:      labels: { component: my-scheduler }    spec:      serviceAccountName: my-scheduler      priorityClassName: system-cluster-critical      topologySpreadConstraints:      - maxSkew: 1        topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone        whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway        labelSelector:          matchLabels: { component: my-scheduler }      containers:      - name: kube-scheduler        image: registry.k8s.io/kube-scheduler:v1.36.0   # match your cluster's version        command:        - kube-scheduler        - --config=/etc/kubernetes/my-scheduler/config.yaml        livenessProbe:          httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 10259, scheme: HTTPS }          initialDelaySeconds: 15        readinessProbe:          httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 10259, scheme: HTTPS }        resources:          requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }          limits:   { memory: 512Mi }        securityContext:          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true          runAsNonRoot: true          runAsUser: 65532          capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }        volumeMounts:        - { name: config, mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/my-scheduler, readOnly: true }      volumes:      - name: config        configMap:          name: my-scheduler-config---apiVersion: policy/v1kind: PodDisruptionBudgetmetadata:  name: my-scheduler  namespace: kube-systemspec:  minAvailable: 1  selector:    matchLabels: { component: my-scheduler }
Going deeper2 points
  • Memory grows with cluster size. The scheduler caches every node and pod. Watch its memory on large clusters and raise the limit before it's OOM-killed, which would leave pods unscheduled until it restarts.
  • Config changes need a restart. kube-scheduler reads its configuration at startup. Roll the Deployment after changing the ConfigMap (a checksum annotation on the pod template does this automatically in GitOps setups).

Step 4: opt workloads in

Scenario. The team adds schedulerName to three batch Deployments by hand. A month later, a new batch job from another team lands on the default scheduler because nobody told them. Opting in should be a property of the namespace, not something every author has to remember.

What the YAML does.

  • Per workload: set schedulerName in the pod template. Here the batch Deployment also tolerates the batch node pool's taint and selects it (see the next section).
  • Per namespace, automatically: a mutating admission policy (Kyverno here) sets schedulerName on every new pod in namespaces labelled scheduling.example.com/profile: binpack, so teams opt in once, at the namespace.
apiVersion: apps/v1kind: Deploymentmetadata:  name: nightly-etl  namespace: batchspec:  replicas: 40  selector:    matchLabels: { app: nightly-etl }  template:    metadata:      labels: { app: nightly-etl }    spec:      schedulerName: affinity-first-scheduler      nodeSelector:        workload-class: batch      tolerations:      - { key: workload-class, value: batch, effect: NoSchedule }      containers:      - name: etl        image: my-company/etl:2.3        resources:          requests: { cpu: "4", memory: 8Gi }---# Opt in a whole namespace instead of editing every workloadapiVersion: kyverno.io/v1kind: ClusterPolicymetadata:  name: batch-namespaces-use-binpack-schedulerspec:  rules:  - name: set-scheduler-name    match:      any:      - resources:          kinds: ["Pod"]          namespaceSelector:            matchLabels: { scheduling.example.com/profile: binpack }    mutate:      patchStrategicMerge:        spec:          schedulerName: affinity-first-scheduler
Going deeper2 points
  • The mutation must happen at creation, because schedulerName is immutable. Existing pods keep their scheduler until they're replaced.
  • Exclude what shouldn't move: DaemonSet pods are placed by their own controller logic and don't need this, and system namespaces should never be labelled for opt-in.

Giving it its own nodes

Scenario. After a week, the team sees a handful of batch pods fail with OutOfcpu right after being scheduled. Both schedulers were placing pods on the same nearly full nodes at the same moment. The fix is to keep them out of each other's way.

What the picture shows. Two node pools, and how taints and selectors keep each scheduler on its own.

1The batch pool is tainted
workload-class=batch:NoSchedule. Pods from the default scheduler don't tolerate it, so they never land there.
2Batch pods tolerate the taint and select the pool
with a nodeSelector, so the second scheduler only places them on batch nodes.
3No overlap, no race
each scheduler is the only writer to its own nodes, so they can't make conflicting placements.
4Each pool has its own Karpenter NodePool
the batch pool can use Spot and aggressive consolidation without affecting services.
apiVersion: karpenter.sh/v1kind: NodePoolmetadata:  name: batchspec:  template:    metadata:      labels:        workload-class: batch    spec:      taints:      - { key: workload-class, value: batch, effect: NoSchedule }      requirements:      - { key: karpenter.sh/capacity-type, operator: In, values: ["spot", "on-demand"] }      - { key: karpenter.k8s.aws/instance-category, operator: In, values: ["c", "m"] }      nodeClassRef:        group: karpenter.k8s.aws        kind: EC2NodeClass        name: default  disruption:    consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized    consolidateAfter: 2m  limits:    cpu: "2000"
Going deeper2 points
  • DaemonSets still run everywhere they tolerate, on both pools. Their pods are part of every node's capacity, and both schedulers account for them.
  • Shared pools are possible if you accept the occasional rejected pod. For pods managed by a controller the cost is a short delay while it's recreated; for bare pods it's a failure you'll have to handle.

Autoscaling with a second scheduler

Scenario. The batch pool is empty overnight. At 2 a.m., 40 batch pods are created, and the team wants Karpenter to launch nodes for them. Does Karpenter even notice pods that belong to a different scheduler?

What the picture shows. How a pod handled by the second scheduler gets a new node.

1Step 1, the pod is created
with schedulerName: affinity-first-scheduler.
2Step 2, the second scheduler tries and fails
no node fits, so it sets the pod's PodScheduled condition to False with reason Unschedulable.
3Step 3, Karpenter reacts to that condition
it watches for pods marked unschedulable, whichever scheduler marked them, works out which NodePool can host them and launches nodes.
4Step 4, the new node registers,
and the second scheduler's next attempt finds room and binds the pod.
5If the second scheduler is down, nothing happens
the pod is never marked unschedulable, so Karpenter never sees it. That's why the scheduler's own availability matters so much.
Going deeper3 points
  • Karpenter simulates with its own logic, which respects the pod's constraints (requests, selectors, affinity, tolerations) but not your scheduler's scoring. Karpenter decides how many nodes to buy; your scheduler then decides which pod goes where.
  • Consolidation can move your pods: when Karpenter removes an underused node, the evicted pods are recreated and placed again by whichever scheduler their schedulerName names. Bin-packing at placement and consolidation later point in the same direction, so they work well together.
  • Cluster Autoscaler also reacts to unschedulable pods, and simulates placement with the scheduler's filter plugins. It has the same blind spot for custom scoring.

Checking that it works, and troubleshooting

Scenario. On Monday a developer says "my pods have been Pending since Friday". The on-call engineer needs a fixed sequence of checks that finds the cause in minutes.

What the picture shows. A troubleshooting path for a pod that's stuck in Pending.

1Is the pod asking for the right scheduler?
kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.spec.schedulerName}'. A typo means no scheduler will ever pick it up.
2Is the scheduler running and leading?
kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l component=my-scheduler shows the replicas; kubectl -n kube-system get lease affinity-first-scheduler shows the current holder. No holder means leader election is failing (check the lease permissions from Step 1).
3Are there any events?
kubectl describe pod <pod>. No events at all means no scheduler has looked at it. A FailedScheduling event from affinity-first-scheduler means it looked and nothing fit; the message lists why (insufficient CPU, untolerated taint, affinity).
4Is autoscaling reacting?
For Unschedulable pods, check Karpenter's logs or NodeClaims for a launch. No NodeClaim means no NodePool matches the pod's constraints.
5Did it get placed by the right scheduler?
kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Scheduled lists each placement with the scheduler that made it.
Going deeper2 points
  • Metrics to alert on: the scheduler exposes Prometheus metrics on port 10259, including scheduler_pending_pods (by queue), scheduler_schedule_attempts_total (by result and profile) and scheduler_scheduling_attempt_duration_seconds. Alert when pending pods for your profile grow while the scheduler's attempt rate is zero: that's a stopped scheduler.
  • Raise the log level temporarily (--v=4) to see each filter's verdict per node, then turn it back down; it's very verbose.

Operating it over time

Scenario. A year later, the cluster has been upgraded three times and the second scheduler is still on the version it was installed with. A new pod field added in the latest release is silently ignored by it. A second scheduler is a control-plane component, and it needs the same care.

What to keep in mind.

  • Upgrade with the cluster: bump the scheduler image to match each control-plane upgrade, in the same change. A scheduler older than the API server may not understand newer pod fields, and quietly places pods as if those fields weren't there.
  • Review the configuration API on upgrades: kubescheduler.config.k8s.io/v1 is stable, but plugins and defaults change between releases; read the scheduler section of the release notes.
  • Keep it in Git: the ServiceAccount, roles, ConfigMap, Deployment, PDB and opt-in policy are one unit. Deploy them together through the same pipeline as the rest of the platform.
  • Know how to back out: removing the opt-in policy and the schedulerName from pod templates sends workloads back to the default scheduler on their next rollout. Keep that path tested.
Failure What you see What to do
Scheduler pods down Opted-in pods Pending with no events; no scale-up Two replicas, PDB, alert on pending pods with zero attempts
Leader election failing Both replicas running, nothing scheduled, "forbidden" in logs Check the lease Role and resourceName match
Version behind the cluster New pod fields ignored Upgrade the image with every cluster upgrade
Shared nodes with the default scheduler Occasional OutOfcpu or OutOfmemory pod failures Give it its own tainted node pool
Typo in schedulerName One workload Pending forever, no events Use the namespace opt-in policy instead of hand-edited names

Facts about Kubernetes, Kueue and AWS reflect public documentation at the time of writing.
